abstractText:
Mammalian genomes are folded into 3-dimensional (3D) structures in the nucleus. How the 2-meter-long primate DNA with 3-billion base pairs (bp) fit into a 10-micrometer nucleus has intrigued biologists for decades. Microscopy imaging and DNA sequencing methods have revealed distinct structural units of DNA territories and domains, which change dynamically when cells change fate or are under environmental stress. How these DNA structural domains functionally impact gene expression and cellular activity remains unclear. To address this important question, the project aims to develop a new CRISPR-based technology platform to reveal the causal relationship between the 3D genome organization and gene expression. The project will develop an online education platform consisting of hands-on curricula modules designed to stimulate broad interest on CRISPR gene editing among undergraduates and high school students. Students from diverse cultural or socio-economic backgrounds will gain exposure to cutting-edge genome editing tools, knowledge and techniques via the remote learning platform. These educational activities are expected to engage STEM students and teachers, promote participation of underrepresented groups, and inform and educate the public about the importance and responsible use of novel gene editing biotechnologies. The project will train graduate students in the field of genome editing and genomics for science communication, education and research.

The research objective of the project is to develop a novel CRISPR-based technology platform to elucidate dynamics and timescales of 3D chromatin interactions and their causal relationship to gene transcription. Preliminary work in the PIs lab has developed several CRISPR-based methods such as LiveFISH for live cell imaging, CRISPRa/i for transcription perturbation, and CRISPR-GO for inducible and reversable repositioning of genomic loci. The project will develop an integrated platform enabling simultaneous perturbation and multi-color imaging of any DNA/RNA/protein on super-resolution level over longitudinal timescales in single living neuron cells. Using induced human neurons as a model system, the specific scientific goals are to: 1) measure the timescales of chromatin looping at signal-stimulated gene loci via live-cell imaging in single neurons; 2) study dynamics of loop formation, mRNA transcription and protein translation via multiple-color super-resolution imaging after neuronal activation; 3) determine the mutual relationship between looping and transcription by targeted perturbation of gene transcription with CRISPRa/i or targeted perturbation of looping with CRISPR-GO. Successful completion of the project will reveal new knowledge of the chromatin loop formation and complexity and uncover their causal functional relationship to transcription and cell activity. The insights gained by this research are expected to form the biotechnology basis that can be used to manipulate and engineer the 3D genome for future functional genomics research. The project is jointly funded by the Systems and Synthetic Biology and Genetic Mechanisms clusters of the MCB Division.

abstractText:
Although pandemics have threatened human civilization since ancient times, how to predict and prevent them remains a pressing challenge, calling for innovative insights and practices. Pandemics emerge through incidental ‘perfect storms’: molecular changes in pathogens, gradual trends in climate, subtle shifts in ecological interactions among potential hosts, and individual behavioral decisions by people, all colluding to make up the difference between an interesting but rare new variant of a known disease and an existential worldwide crisis. Being able to predict the emergence of pandemic threats, therefore, requires a fully integrated, multidisciplinary approach, able to consider the complexity of these realms across scales of interaction to predict and, ideally, prevent.  This workshop is one of four bringing experts from scholarly communities in the social and behavioral sciences, biology, engineering, and computer science together to discuss how to integrate the approaches taken by each community into a more effective, unified science of pandemic prediction.  The focus of this workshop is on developing understanding of how human attitudes, social behavior, and the drivers underlying both shape patterns of infectious-disease transmission and efforts at control and eradication.  This fundamental understanding in turn will facilitate pandemic prevention and control decisions that leave us better prepared when confronted with future pandemic threats.

The workshop is structured to focus on four topical areas of crucial importance, dealing with cultural transmission, information and communication, equity, and sustainability. The white paper that comes from this workshop will provide important guidance for incorporating insights into the social and behavioral sciences into predictive intelligence and pandemic prevention.   It will inform future research investments, institutional capacity-building, and other policy priorities aimed at keeping the US and the world safe from inevitable future pandemics.

projectOutComesReport:
We convened the NSF Predictive Intelligence for Pandemic Prevention (PIPP) “Human” Workshop in March 22-23rd, 2021, to gather information on what is currently known about the human dimensions of pandemic preparedness and control and where the gaps lie. The workshop virtually brought together over 250 researchers and practitioners from diverse fields.

Human behavior is central to the origins, transmission, and control of infectious disease. Population and economic forces, both of which are aggregate outcomes of human behavior, lead to the conversion of wildlands, expanding the human-animal interface where zoonotic spillover becomes more likely. Livelihood-related behavior exposes people to potential zoonotic spillover and mobility moves spillover infections to population centers where they can establish a foothold in human populations. Every transmission of an infectious disease is a social event: by whatever the appropriate mechanism, a susceptible individual must make contact with an infectious one. Norms, customs, social rules, and policies structure who interacts with whom and therefore leave traces of who gets sick and who is spared. Control of infectious disease depends critically on reducing effective contacts within the suspected population. Once again, cultural norms, customs, social structure, risk attitudes, and government policies play a fundamental role in the success of control and mitigation measures. Given the clear centrality of human behavior and social organization to infectious disease, it is surprising how few formal linkages exist between the social sciences and pandemic-control policy.

Despite the centrality of human behavior to both the origins and control of pandemics, it is strangely absent – and frequently discounted – in both scientific and policy discussions of pandemics. A common refrain throughout the COVID-19 pandemic was some variation on the statement that "the science is clear; it's human behavior that's the problem." Naturally, this statement belies the fact that there is, in fact, a science of human behavior and that if human behavior is the "problem," it should be incorporated more broadly into the science of pandemics. 

A major obstacle for further development of an integrative pandemic science that incorporates human behavior is the dearth of scholars with expertise in both the social sciences and some aspect of pandemic prediction and control.

The Human-PIPP Workshop included four substantive sessions on topics of social relevance for pandemics. These included: (1) Cultural Transmission, Identity, and Groups, (2) Equity, Access, and Community Engagement, (3) Information, Communication, and Misinformation, and (4) Sustainability, Longevity, and Institutional Memory of Preparations. The workshop was capped off by a summary session.

We concluded the workshop by identifying four Grand Challenges for incorporating the behavioral and social sciences into pandemic prediction, prevention, and control:

  1. Incorporate the models and insights of the social and behavioral sciences into the mathematical and computational models used to forecast, predict, and develop interventions for pandemics. This goal goes beyond incorporating increasingly fine-grained mobility data into such models. Rather, it is about generating theory-driven models capable of reflecting, for example, scientific understanding of behavior change, social structure, and economic inequality into these important tools for pandemic prediction, prevention, and control.
  2. Develop strategies to increase trust. Trust at multiple levels is essential for pandemic control: there is the need for trust of institutions such as the different levels of government, with more abstract institutions such as science and public health, within and between communities. The breakdown of trust in US society has made controlling the COVID-19 pandemic far more difficult than it otherwise would have been. There are substantial challenges for cultivating trust in highly heterogeneous populations and, since the diversity of society is unlikely to decrease in the future, developing strategies that foster trust in heterogeneous societies should be a major priority moving forward.
  3. Combat health misinformation. This involves understanding why people (or particular groups of people at particular times) are susceptible to misinformation as well as developing strategies to combat misinformation in real time. This would require going from mechanistic models of misinformation transmission, to utilizing and advancing theories in different pertinent disciplines (e.g., cognitive science, information science, psychology, public health) to identify why such misinformation spreads, and how it can be countered.
  4. Developing research networks that bring together scientists from epidemiology, biology, mathematical and computational sciences, and the social and behavioral sciences. The scale and complexity of pandemics require multidisciplinary approaches to science and policy. Achieving success in answering grand challenges will require a rethinking of the social organization of relevant science. Approaches similar to the NASA matrix organization system may hold promise but what is clear is that this organization will need to span existing institutions since no one institution possesses the critical mass necessary.

abstractText:
The aim of this proposal is to enable people to control robots remotely using virtual reality. Using cameras mounted on the robot and a virtual reality headset, a person can see the environment around the robot. However, controlling the robot using existing technologies is hard: there is a time delay because it’s slow to send high quality video over the Internet. In addition, the fidelity of the image is worse than looking through human eyes, with a fixed and narrow view. This proposal will address these limitations by creating a new system which understands the geometry and appearance of the robot’s environment. Instead of sending high-quality video over the Internet, this new system will only send a smaller amount of information about how the environment’s geometry and appearance has changed over time. Further, understanding the geometry and appearance will let us expand the view visible to the person. Overall, these will improve a human’s ability to remotely control the robot by increasing fidelity and responsiveness. We will demonstrate this technology on household tasks, on assembly tasks, and by manipulating small objects.

The aim of this proposal is to test the hypothesis that integrating scene and networking understanding can enable efficient transmission and rendering for dexterous control of remote robots through virtual reality interfaces. This system will result in dexterous teleoperation that enables remote human operators to perform complex tasks with remote robot manipulators, such as cleaning a room or repairing a machine. Such tasks have not previously been demonstrated to be teleoperated for two reasons: 1) lack of an intuitive awareness and understanding of the scene around the remote robot, and 2) lack of an effective low-latency interface to control the robot. We will address these problems by creating new scene- and network-aware algorithms which tightly couple sensing, display, interaction and transmission, enabling the operator to quickly and intuitively understand the environment around the robot. This project will research new interfaces which allow the operator to use their hand to directly specify the robot’s end effector pose in six degrees of freedom, combined with spatial- and semantic-object-based models that allow safe high-level commands. This project will evaluate the proposed system by assessing the speed and accuracy of the remote operator’s ability to complete complex tasks, including assembly tasks; the aim will be to complete unstructured assembly tasks that have never been demonstrated to be remotely teleoperated before.

This project is in response to the NSF Cyber-Physical Systems 20-563 solicitation.

projectOutComesReport:
This project was a collaboration between robotics and graphics researchers at Brown University, and computer networking researchers at Stanford University. We sought to discover and create better ways to remotely operate robots over long distances, over the Internet. One could imagine it might be helpful to be able to remotely operate a vehicle or piece of farm equipment over the Internet, sort laundry or do dishes, or even (in a distant future) remotely change a baby's diaper! Before any of these things would be possible, significant improvement to current technology will be required. In this project, we wanted to test a hypothesis that remotely operating robots could work better if our systems (at sender and receiver) both understood the scene (the environment where the robot was operating) and the network conditions between the two sites.

The Stanford team focused on the network aspect of this problem. One critical aspect is to reduce the apparent end-to-end delay between sender (the human operator) and receiver (the robot), because it is hard to manipulate remote objects if there is a substantial delay between human intention and the apparent robot action of carrying out those intentions. We explored ways for components within the network (e.g. routers in the Internet) to "help" long-distance connections achieve lower end-to-end delay.

One of our research papers was published at the USENIX Network Systems Design & Implementation 2024 conference ("Sidekick: In-Network Assistance for Secure End-to-End Transport Protocols"); we discovered and described new mathematical techniques for Internet infrastructure to "help" long-distance connections. We published a second research paper at the USENIX 2025 Annual Technical Conference ("Internet Connection Splitting: What's Old is New Again"), reporting measurement results that document the necessity of this "help" even for the most modern techniques for long-distance ("end-to-end") communication. A third research paper is currently in preparation, in which we designed and describe even better techniques for this in-network assistance in different situations.

In future work, we and other researchers will need to combine these techniques with the best low-delay visualizations of the remote robot to allow "dexterous" manipulation of far-away environments.

abstractText:
The broader impact of this I-Corps program is the development of bioluminescence tools that may be applied to drug discovery and optimization, particularly for the non-invasive imaging of animals. To date, bioluminescence imaging in the pharmaceutical industry has been limited due to poor light penetrance and enzyme instability. Fundamental research has contributed to the advancement of bioluminescence imaging. The goal is to bridge the gap and expand the use of bioluminescent reporters. Specifically, the proposed technology will use biosensors for rapidly evaluating drug candidates in laboratory animals, in addition to cell cultured cells. This technology may have a significant impact on central nervous system (CNS) drug development and accelerate the optimization of drugs for brain malignancies. This tool may lead to improved compounds with better blood brain barrier (BBB) penetrance and better activity in the brain, while also preventing the testing of suboptimal compounds in human volunteers and patients.

This I-Corps project is based on the development of new drug screening platforms that enable non-invasive detection of drug activity and efficacy in living animals. Recently, bioluminescent reporters have been engineered to be brighter and red-shifted, thereby allowing deep tissue imaging of biological events. These molecular tools enable the detection of drug activity in an approach that is label-free, non-invasive, and pathway-specific. In addition, these biosensors may be used to monitor drug activity in living animals, thus circumventing the numerous limitations of terminal analyses. By evaluating targeted drug candidates in vivo, without termination, the performance and efficacy of the compounds can be more accurately appraised. This is especially valuable for optimizing molecules penetrating the central nervous system (CNS), in which the blood-brain barrier (BBB) has presented significant challenges in CNS drug development. The goal of this project is to determine the ways in which these biosensors could facilitate the rapid assessment of CNS compounds, and when these tools may have the most impact in the drug development pipeline.

projectOutComesReport:
The goal of this I-Corps project, "An in vivo central nervous system drug screening platform with noninvasive imaging", was to translate a novel method for drug assessment in vivo into a commercializable service platform. During the project, we performed market research on the specifications a viable product offering would require, contacted potential customers, determined the design of multiple prototypes, and collaborated with researchers to implement the prototypes. 

 

Outcomes of the award occurred stepwise in the two years of the award. In year 1, we honed the product as a suite of services of two types. The first type of service will be bioluminescent reporters for kinase pathways that are major targets for drug screening campaigns in biopharma companies, which can be expressed in the mouse CNS via virus-mediated gene delivery. The second type of service will be custom bioluminescent reporters for specific kinases, requiring only knowledge of a phosphorylation substrate for the kinase, with machine learning-assisted protein engineering. In year 2, we selected three kinase pathways to serve as initial product offerings and, together with collaborating scientists at Stanford University, successfully generated the first prototype drug activty reporter and obtained proof-of-principle of identifying brain-active drugs in mice.

 

Overall, in addition to the technical accomplishments of designing, engineering, and validating a novel method for assessing drug activity in the brain, greater impacts of this project include the training of the four team members in understanding how drug screening-related technologies are evaluated and adopted in the biopharma industry, including assessments of relative performance, market size, and intellectual property. This learning has been vital in the entry of two team members into the biotech industry, one as a product manager in a genomics company and another as an associate at a life sciences venture capital firm.

abstractText:
Located nearly 3000 km below the crust, the Earth’s core is the most remote region within our planet. Mainly composed of iron, the core’s outer shell is liquid while its most inner part, the inner core, is solid.  The core plays a central role in the planet’s geomagnetism, dynamic processes, and thermal evolution. Here, the team conducts laboratory experiments at the extreme pressures and temperatures prevailing in Earth’s deep interior.  They measure the properties of the iron-rich materials that make up the core, e.g., their deformation mechanisms and viscosity.  These properties can be dramatically altered at core conditions. The results give insight into why seismic waves travel at different speeds through different parts of the inner core. They constrain how the Earth’s magnetic field is generated and unveil its past evolution. These outcomes are valuable to many researchers studying deep Earth’s processes: mineral physicists, seismologists, and geodynamicists. The project promotes technical advances useful across disciplines, in geoscience and materials science, and in the industry. It also provides support for a female graduate student, training for undergraduate students, and outreach toward K-12 students and the public.

The project aims at characterizing key rheological properties of iron and iron-rich compounds and alloys at the extreme conditions of the deep Earth. Two fundamental questions are addressed: (1) What causes inner-core seismic anisotropy? (2) How does viscous dissipation in the outer core influence the evolution of the geodynamo? To address the first question, the team characterizes the dominant deformation mechanisms and strength of solid iron at high pressures and temperatures. The lattice preferred orientation that develops during iron crystallization is also measured. The goal is to understand how the alignment of elastically anisotropic iron crystals may be acquired during solidification or subsequent deformation (or both).  To this aim, the researchers carry out static compression experiments in resistive and laser-heated diamond anvil cells. They perform in situ X-ray imaging and diffraction measurements at national synchrotron facilities.  Addressing the second question requires measuring iron viscosity at core conditions. While traditional measurements are limited to lower pressures, the team benefit from new technical developments; these enable a path toward measuring the viscosity of iron dynamically compressed to outer core conditions. Thus the team carries out dynamic compression experiments and use novel X-ray diffraction and imaging techniques at the Materials at Extreme Conditions instrument at the Linac Coherent Light Source (SLAC) and the National Ignition Facility at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. These experiments represent new opportunities to leverage the considerable resources and expertise available at national laboratories and apply them to better understand the Earth.

projectOutComesReport:
NSF Award: Geophysics of Iron in the Earth's Core (2021-2025)

This project advanced our fundamental understanding of iron and iron-rich materials under the extreme pressure and temperature conditions relevant to Earth's deep interior. Using cutting-edge experimental techniques at major national facilities, we investigated two critical questions: (1) What causes seismic anisotropy in Earth's inner core? and (2) How does viscous flow in the outer core influence the geodynamo that generates Earth's magnetic field?

By revealing the microscopic mechanisms controlling iron's behavior under extreme conditions, our experiments provide essential input parameters for computational models of planetary core formation, magnetic field generation, and the long-term thermal evolution of rocky planets—both in our solar system and around other stars. The techniques we developed establish new standards for studying materials under extreme conditions and will continue advancing our understanding of matter under the pressures and temperatures found in planetary interiors throughout the universe.

This project resulted in peer-reviewed publications in journals including Nature Communications, Scientific Reports, Physical Review Letters, and Meteoritics & Planetary Science. Our work on iron deformation was featured as an Editor's Suggestion in Physical Review Letters and highlighted on their website.

 

Major results:

We achieved the first-ever femtosecond-scale visualization of iron's deformation under shock compression using ultrafast, radial X-ray diffraction at the Linac Coherent Light Source, revealing that twinning—not dislocations as previously assumed—controls iron's behavior at extreme strain rates. This discovery fundamentally changes our understanding of how metals deform under planetary impact conditions and provides new constraints for modeling Earth's core formation. Also using ultrafast X-ray diffraction at the Linac Coherent Light Source, we provided the first direct experimental evidence of silicon's deformation mechanism under laser-driven shock compression. This resolved a decades-old debate about whether phase transitions occur through plastic deformation or inelastic shear-release mechanisms.

Using the National Ignition Facility's unprecedented capabilities, we measured iron's strength at 400 GPa pressure and 5000 K temperature—conditions approaching Earth's inner core. Surprisingly, we found that different starting iron microstructures (single crystal vs. polycrystalline) exhibit dramatically different strengths at these extreme conditions, with implications for understanding inner core anisotropy.

We demonstrated that the rate of compression significantly affects phase transitions in iron-nickel alloys, with transition pressures varying from 12.5 GPa at slow rates to 13.6 GPa at rapid compression. This finding has profound implications for understanding how planetary materials behave during giant impacts versus gradual accretion.

We developed novel experimental approaches combining X-ray free electron lasers with shock compression, enabling simultaneous structural and electronic characterization of materials on femtosecond timescales. These techniques now serve as benchmarks for studying planetary formation processes and extreme materials behavior. By combining X-ray imaging with diffraction, we achieved the first direct visualization of high-pressure phase nucleation and growth at the nanoscale, providing temporal constraints on deformation kinetics that can be directly compared to state-of-the-art simulations.

Our findings provide new constraints for models of Earth's magnetic field generation and inner core evolution. The discovery that iron's strength varies dramatically with microstructure helps explain seismic observations of inner core anisotropy and informs models of core crystallization during Earth's thermal evolution.

Broader impacts:

The project supported comprehensive training for early-career scientists: one postdoctoral researcher secured a faculty position in France, one graduate students completed their PhD, one completed a MS, and multiple undergraduate students and high school interns gained hands-on experience with cutting-edge experimental techniques.

The project leveraged major national facilities including the Advanced Photon Source, SLAC's Linac Coherent Light Source, Lawrence Livermore's National Ignition Facility, and the OMEGA Laser Facility, strengthening collaborative networks across multiple institutions and advancing experimental capabilities at these world-class facilities.

While focused on Earth science questions, our experimental techniques and findings impact materials science, planetary science, and high-energy density physics. The methods we developed can be applied to study everything from industrial materials processing to conditions in exoplanet interiors.

abstractText:
Algorithm design is the study of techniques for efficient computation on large-scale problems. Modern industries rely on computational problems ranging from statistical analysis of massive amounts of data to optimization problems that improve their ongoing operations. As such, general-purpose frameworks for designing fast and reliable algorithms are very valuable. Linear and convex programming is one such framework, studied since the 1830s by mathematicians, and since the 1940s as a tool for solving computational problems. Modern applications of convex programming can be found everywhere; for example, power companies optimize their pricing and sourcing of electricity, and companies like Uber and Amazon optimize their logistics, using convex programming. More recently, convexity has played an important role in statistical and probabilistic analysis; there is an increasing amount of interest in these problems due to their intimate connection with and uses in machine learning. While convexity and convex programming have had many successes, they are only suited for continuous problems, leaving a large gap to address discrete phenomena. Discrete phenomena can be found everywhere: statistical models of diseases and symptoms in medicine, categorical predictions in machine-learning models, and value-optimization problems involving bundling of items in retail industries. The goal of this project is to develop a foundational framework for fast and reliable statistical-analysis and optimization algorithms based on discrete notions of convexity for discrete problems. This project incorporates a synergistic education plan that includes curriculum development for undergraduate and graduate students at Stanford university aimed at students from a diverse set of areas: computer science, statistics, mathematics, and operations research.

This project will develop a discrete convexity framework for algorithm design through three fronts. First, the project will study combinatorics of convex polytopes encapsulating discrete objects and relate them to algorithmic efficiency. The project will explore generalization of matroids, objects widely used in combinatorial optimization because of their theoretical guarantees in greedy algorithms. The expected outcome will be an understanding of when local search, an optimization technique that operates by changing small parts of the solution at a time, succeeds. Second, the project will explore randomized algorithms such as Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Gibbs Sampling on discrete objects, producing an understanding of when local algorithms are successful in sampling from discrete distributions and in statistical analysis. One goal of this project is connecting the effectiveness of local search for optimization problems and local algorithms for sampling from probability distributions. Finally, the project will explore variational techniques for statistical analysis, a category of convex-programming-based algorithms that are typically much faster than Markov Chain Monte Carlo, but sometimes come with worse theoretical guarantees; however, variational techniques are widely used with success in practice, and this project will aim at shedding light on their effectiveness through the lens of discrete convexity. This project is interdisciplinary and will provide connections between computer science and other fields, most notably statistics, combinatorics, algebraic geometry.

abstractText:
This project examines the effects of COVID-19 exposure during pregnancy on birth outcomes, over time, and across different groups defined by different sources of disadvantage.  The COVID-19 pandemic is a large shock likely to affect infant health through multiple pathways including maternal infection, stress and anxiety, economic hardship, and access to prenatal care. Because these factors differ across groups in the United States, the impact of COVID-19 on birth outcomes will likely be stronger among groups with fewer advantages and certain demographic groups, exacerbating differences in the United States.  These effects are critical to understand because birth outcomes predict health and socioeconomic attainment throughout the life course. 

This study relies on causal inference techniques exploiting variation in infection rates across time and place to capture the consequences of the pandemic on differences in birth outcomes, in particular intrauterine growth restriction, a key predictor of early-life cognition, education, and ultimately earnings.  Birth records obtained at the state level with early release are used to provide the earliest possible evidence.  Research focuses on six states that provide large and diverse samples across areas where the pandemic has unfolded with significant variation.  Time-varying data on COVID incidence and mortality, and local official responses are linked to these data.

This project examined how the COVID-19 pandemic affected infant health and fertility in the United States. The pandemic represented a major social and public health shock, and this research sought to understand how exposure to COVID-19 illness and the broader disruptions associated with the pandemic influenced birth outcomes and the wellbeing of the next generation.

The research focused on three main questions. First, it examined whether exposure to COVID-19 during pregnancy affected infant health at birth. Outcomes studied included gestational age, preterm birth, birth weight, low birth weight, and intrauterine growth restriction. These outcomes are important predictors of children’s health, development, and wellbeing over the life course. Second, the project analyzed whether the effects of COVID-19 exposure differed across social groups, including differences by maternal age, race and ethnicity, socioeconomic disadvantage, and community socioeconomic conditions. Third, the research examined whether the pandemic influenced fertility patterns, including changes in the number and characteristics of women giving birth, which can shape population-level trends in infant health.

To address these questions, the research team assembled and analyzed large population-level datasets containing birth records from multiple U.S. states, including Alabama, Alaska, California, and New Jersey. These administrative data allow researchers to study birth outcomes for entire populations without selectivity and to identify even rare but serious outcomes such as extremely preterm birth. The project used rigorous statistical and causal inference methods to distinguish the effects of COVID-19 illness and pandemic-related disruptions from other factors affecting infant health.

The project generated several important findings. First, the research provides strong evidence that maternal COVID-19 infection during pregnancy increases the risk of preterm and very preterm birth. Second, the project shows that the effects of the pandemic on infant health were not evenly distributed. Instead, the consequences varied across social groups and communities, highlighting how social and economic inequalities shape health risks during major public health crises. Third, the research demonstrates that COVID-19 vaccination substantially reduced the negative effects of maternal infection on infant health, underscoring the importance of vaccination as a strategy to protect both mothers and newborns. Fourth, the study showed that the pandemic resulted in a short-term decline in number of births among some groups with a rapid recovery to baseline rates.

The findings from this project have been widely disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, academic conferences, and research seminars. Articles from the project have appeared in leading scientific journals including Demography, Population and Development Review, and Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. One article on vaccination and infant health received a prestigious award from the National Academy of Sciences. It also received substantial public attention and was covered by more than one hundred news outlets worldwide, helping to inform broader public discussions about the pandemic’s impacts.

The project also contributed to the training of the next generation of researchers. Ten graduate and undergraduate students participated in the project as research assistants. Students gained experience in literature review, quantitative data analysis, and spatial analysis, and worked collaboratively with faculty investigators. These activities provided valuable training in population health research and advanced quantitative methods.

Overall, this research improves our understanding of how major social disruptions affect the earliest stages of life. By combining large-scale population data with rigorous analytical methods, the project provides new evidence on the health consequences of the COVID-19 pandemic and the role of public health interventions such as vaccination in protecting vulnerable populations.

abstractText:
The overarching goal of this project is to understand how cell growth triggers cell division. It has long been known that there is often a requirement for cell growth in order to initiate cell division, but the way this works has remained unknown. The central question is what is biochemically different about a large cell compared to a small cell that makes it divide? To address this question, this project is based on a recent breakthrough by the investigator in understanding how growth triggers division in budding yeast. Contrary to expectations, the investigator found that growth did not increase the activity of a cell division activator. Instead, cell growth triggers division by diluting a protein that inhibits cell division. This project leverages this conceptual breakthrough to rephrase the question of how cell growth triggers cell division to the question of how cell growth results in different amounts of specific proteins being made. In other words, what are the mechanisms that ensure that proteins activating cell division are made in proportion to the size of the cell so that their concentrations do not change as cells get larger? Moreover, how do big and small cells make the same number of cell division inhibitors so that their concentrations decrease as cells grow larger to trigger division? By answering these questions, this project will determine the molecular mechanisms cells use to link cell growth to cell division, which is a fundamental question in cell and developmental biology.  The Broader Impact of the project includes the intrinsic nature of the research as all dividing cells need to regulate cell size.  Additional activities include the training of undergraduate and graduate students along with post-doctoral researchers.  Activities to broadly promote quantitative training along with outreach to high school students will also be carried out. 

Cell growth, division, and biosynthesis must be carefully orchestrated to maintain efficient cellular function. To achieve this, cell size and biosynthesis are inextricably linked. Total RNA and protein synthesis rates increase in proportion to size so that gene product copy numbers scale with cell volume. This ensures that macromolecule concentrations are kept constant as a cell grows to maintain efficient cellular function. However, if cells become excessively large, this scaling of biosynthesis collapses and cellular physiology and efficient growth become severely compromised. To prevent this, budding yeast cells maintain their size within an optimal range for cellular function by coupling cell growth to cell division. The researchers found that the synthesis of the cell cycle activator Cln3 increased in proportion to cell size, while the synthesis of the budding yeast cell cycle inhibitor Whi5 was independent of cell size such that a constant number of Whi5 molecules are made in each cell cycle. Thus, Whi5 concentration is more dilute in larger cells which triggers an earlier cell cycle entry in larger cells. Thus, the differential size-dependencies of cell cycle activators, which scale in proportion to cell size, and cell cycle inhibitors, which are independent of cell size, couple growth to division to maintain cells within a physiologically optimal size range. The differential size-dependencies in the synthesis of cell cycle activators and inhibitors raise two key questions will be addressed in this project. First, what ensures most protein and mRNA synthesis increases in proportion to cell size? Second, what allows proteins, such as Whi5, to break the general rule and be expressed independently of cell size? This project will employ the model organism budding yeast to address these twin questions using a combination of proteomics, genetics, and quantitative live cell imaging. Successful completion of the project will thereby resolve a fundamental question in cell biology of how cell size, cell division, and biosynthesis are intimately and mechanistically linked to promote cellular function.

Cell growth, division, and biosynthesis must be carefully orchestrated to maintain efficient cellular function. To achieve this, cell size and biosynthesis are inextricably linked. Imagine each cell as a bustling factory where size and biosynthesis are closely intertwined. As these cells grow, their demand for building blocks—RNA and proteins—increases proportionally to fuel their expansion. This ensures that macromolecule concentrations are kept constant as a cell grows to maintain efficient cellular function. Yet, if cells balloon beyond a certain point, this delicate balance is upset, throwing cellular physiology into disarray and stunting efficient growth. To avoid this, cells employ a clever strategy: they tether their growth to the process of division, ensuring they stay within an optimal size range.

 

While it has long been clear that cell size, cell division, and biosynthesis are intimately linked, the underlying molecular mechanisms have been unclear. How proportional synthesis of RNA arises is especially mysterious because the template DNA content increases abruptly while transcription increases continuously as a cell grows. Thus, the key to the question of how biosynthesis scales with cell size is to understand how transcription scales in proportion to cell size?

 

This research project has unveiled some of the secrets to how transcription is scaled in proportion to cell size. We discovered that while other components of the transcription machinery play minor roles, RNA polymerase II—the enzyme responsible for transcribing messenger RNA—emerges as the primary player, regulating transcription rates nearly in proportion with cell size. However, contrary to previous theories, our findings reveal that RNA polymerase activity doesn't quite scale in proportion to cell size as required. Instead, it follows a dynamic equilibrium model, where the rate of polymerase loading is tied to the concentration of unengaged polymerases in the cell's nucleus. However, this results in an undershoot of the required linear production required to maintain RNA in proportion to cell size, which is then remedied by a compensatory increase in RNA stability as cells get larger. Taken together, our results show how limiting RNA polymerase and feedback on RNA stability work in concert to ensure the precise scaling of RNA amounts across the physiological cell size range.

abstractText:
With establishment of an agreed-upon legal definition of refugee as a person with a “well-founded fear of past and future persecution,” recognizing fear, evaluating its plausibility and verifying its rationality has been at the core of asylum law in the more than 145 countries signatories of the United Nations Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees. Although researchers have been concerned with the interpretation of emotions in immigration law, no particular attention has been placed to the development of policy instruments that aim to differentiate legal fear of persecution from psychological trauma. A better understanding of what makes someone fearful in the eyes of the law can inform U.S. efforts to promulgate sound legal practices that accounts for the complexities of translating experiences into legal and medical evidence. In addition to contributing to the training of a graduate student in the methods of empirical, scientific data collection and analysis, the project would enhance scientific understanding by broadly disseminating its findings to organizations invested in discovering more effective methods for communicating science around legal practice to the public. The project would also broaden the participation of groups historically underrepresented in science. 

This project explores how medical and psychological science related to trauma is engaged in evidentiary proceedings related to asylum claims. During twelve months of a sociolegal and ethnographic context with a high concentration of refugees (and thus appropriately saturated to constitute a representative study population), the researcher will examine the entirety of asylum process, observing the day-to-day activities of government officials, attorneys, asylum seekers, medical expert witnesses, and organizational staff. She will specifically analyze narrations of fear in asylum interviews, evaluations of fear in medico-legal reports, and evidence of fear in asylum decisions. Data will be collected using archival research, interviews, and participant observation in a range of governmental, legal, and peri-governmental contexts. The findings of this research will help advance the study of legal culture, bureaucratic institutions, and policy practices where law and medicine meet.

projectOutComesReport:
With the establishment of the legal definition of refugee as a person with a “well-founded fear of past and future persecution,” recognizing fear, evaluating its plausibility, and verifying its rationality has been at the core of asylum law in the countries that adhere to the United Nations Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees. Although researchers have been concerned with the interpretation of emotions in immigration law, no particular attention has been placed on the development of policy instruments that aim to differentiate legal fear of persecution from psychological trauma. This project contributes to a better understanding of what makes someone fearful in the eyes of the law. Therefore, it informs U.S. efforts to promulgate sound legal practices that account for the complexity of translating lived experiences into legal and medical evidence.  

During twelve months of a sociolegal and ethnographic context with a high concentration of asylum seekers (and thus appropriately saturated to constitute a representative study population), the researcher examined the entirety of the asylum petition process, observing the day-to-day activities of government officials, attorneys, asylum seekers, medical expert witnesses, and administrative staff. The investigator has specifically analyzed narrations of fear in asylum interviews, evaluations of fear in medico-legal reports, and evidence of fear in asylum decisions. Data was collected using archival research, interviews, and participant observation in various governmental, legal, and peri-governmental contexts.

This project helps advance the study of legal culture, bureaucratic institutions, and policy practices where law and medicine meet. During the past two decades, scholars have examined how the interpretation of emotions is a critical component of decision-making in immigration law. However, there are no studies on how the judgment of fear plays a critical role in determining who is granted legal personhood in asylum law. By investigating the judicialization of fear, or how it is made into a legal object, this project not only contributes to the scholarship focused on asylum and bureaucracy but also aims to expand the role of current research on debates about how law and policy are made when institutions develop instruments to measure emotions. By observing how fear is interpreted in medical terms in the context of immigration law, this project participates in the interdisciplinary analysis of medico-legal reports, therapeutic techniques, and ideas of competency in legal contexts. Therefore, this research offers new perspectives by inquiring into the distinction between legal fear of persecution and psychological diagnoses of post-traumatic stress disorder, trauma, and psychosis.

Various disciplines have used ethnographic methods to study fear. However, these “ethnographies of fear” have mainly touched upon how fear is used to induce social responses. By following how fear is identified, measured, assessed, and evaluated in immigration law, this ethnographic work asks how different ideas of fear contain moral values, political valences, and judgments of who is worthy of rights. By studying cases of immigrants with diagnoses related to trauma, post-traumatic stress disorder, psychosis, and pathological fear, this study contributes to interdisciplinary efforts to understand the experience of people with mental disabilities.

This project also contributes to the new conversations on the potential of digital ethnography and digital humanities. The impact of the Covid-19 pandemic on this project resulted in the design of methods that ultimately advance the endeavor to find a meeting point between technology, ethnography, and social scientific analysis. By sharing the researcher’s experience in conducting ethnography through digital and hybrid methods—including court observation and hearing preparation meetings—this project will contribute to the rising interest in the field of digital ethnography. Additionally, incorporating computational science methodologies into analyzing a large corpus of legal documents has created a synergy between ethnographic methods and computational data analysis that is otherwise undermined or not explored. The researcher has treated computational text analysis as ethnographic material, which has provoked interest in data and text mining experts who are keen on applying ethnographic knowledge to digital humanities.  

The preliminary results of this research project have been shared at numerous conferences, talks, and panels. The final results will be included in a dissertation format and subsequently as a book for public audiences. In addition to contributing to the training of a graduate student in the methods of empirical, and scientific data collection and analysis, the project enhances scientific understanding by broadly disseminating its findings to organizations invested in discovering more effective methods for communicating science around legal practice. The project will also broaden the participation of groups historically underrepresented in science. The researcher hopes that with the dissemination of this project’s results, the public will develop skills to understand the effect of the judicialization of emotions in the lives of immigrants, especially those leaving from Latin American countries.

abstractText:
Human stem cells can be grown into organ mimics, termed “organoids”. If they can faithfully reproduce the key structures and activities of organs, they would be extremely valuable.  They could revolutionize the way we discover and test new drugs, study human disease, and possibly even replace damaged body parts. The technology to produce consistent and reliable organoids does not exist. This project will combine a novel type of live imaging microscopy with adaptive biomaterials technology to enable active monitoring and manipulation of liver organoids. As part of the project, the investigators will recruit and train diverse students at the high school, undergraduate, and graduate levels. They will also promote science activities to under-served elementary students, and engage in high school educator development.

Three-dimensional (3D) culture of human stem cells as “organoids” has tremendous clinical potential. Applications include drug discovery, safety and efficacy testing, regenerative medicine, and as models of normal and diseased tissue development. An unmet requirement for the success of these applications is proper organoid differentiation and maturation. Through this RECODE project, a noninvasive imaging method to actively monitor human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) will be developed.  This information will be used to manipulate adaptive biomaterials. These biomaterials will modulate matrix-mediated biomechanical and biochemical cues and reproducibly direct organoid differentiation. Finally, the improved reproducibility and functionality of the RECODE-differentiated organoids will be validated through assays that represent the three major potential applications for hepatic organoids: regenerative medicine, drug screening, and disease modeling. The novel technologies developed will have broad applicability to a variety of other cell, organoid, and tissue types.

projectOutComesReport:
This project aimed to enhance the reproducibility of hepatic organoid (HO) cultures by integrating cutting-edge imaging techniques, engineered biomaterials, and stem cell-derived liver organoids. By leveraging human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), our research developed HO models that closely resemble the structure and function of the human liver, enabling studies on liver disease mechanisms and potential therapies.

Intellectual Merit

Our study successfully introduced novel methodologies in imaging, biomaterials engineering, and disease modeling. Advanced nonlinear microscopy techniques - such as coherent anti-Stokes Raman Scattering (CARS), second harmonic generation (SHG), and multi-photon emission fluorescence (MPEF) microscopy - were employed to dynamically monitor organoid differentiation and maturation. These tools allowed for real-time analysis of lipid accumulation and fibrosis development, providing new insights into liver disease progression. Additionally, we developed a novel adaptive hydrogel system that uses small molecule competitors to achieve on-the-fly manipulation of hydrogel properties, helping to reproducibly direct organoid growth and differentiation. By integrating a computational model, we demonstrated that dynamically stiffening hydrogels improve HO formation and differentiation over time. Finally, we applied this system to study the effects of extracellular matrix stiffness on lipid accumulation in a model of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). Our results revealed that increased matrix stiffness enhances lipid accumulation and fibrosis markers, while inhibition of mechanosignaling mitigates these effects. Our in vitro NAFLD model offers opportunities to study mechanosignaling in hepatocytes and identify a potential therapeutic target for liver disease.

Broader Impacts

Beyond scientific advancements, the project provided hands-on training for graduate students and interns in biomaterials engineering, organoid culture, and disease modeling, fostering expertise in cutting-edge research fields. Findings were disseminated through peer-reviewed publications and national conferences, promoting interdisciplinary knowledge exchange. Furthermore, the research has significant translational potential, as the HO-based disease model can serve as a platform for screening therapeutic candidates targeting mechanosignaling pathways in NAFLD, contributing to the future development of liver disease treatments.

abstractText:
With support from the NSF Molecular & Cellular Biosciences, and the NSF 2026 Fund Program in the Office of Integrated Activities, Professors Sindy Tang and Stanley Qi at Stanford University aim to build a tissue-like composite material, and apply biological principles to change the shape, structure, and function of the material. Specifically, the research will develop functional synthetic units that can perform an elemental topological transition, or a rearrangement in the positioning of the function units. Elemental topological transitions are important in the morphogenesis of biological systems, such as tissue development, wound healing, and regeneration. Achieving topological transitions using synthetic components will open new opportunities to attain macroscopic restructuring of the material towards material morphogenesis, and lead to new classes of autonomous, self-structuring, and self-healing Engineered Living Materials (ELMs). This project will provide an opportunity for undergraduate education in an interdisciplinary area, supporting workforce development at the interface of colloidal physics, material science, microfluidics, and DNA technology, not possible in traditional, single discipline-based training. 

Biological systems are masters in building complex structures and programming shape changes. Macroscopic shape changes in tissues, or morphogenesis, is composed of a set of elemental topological transitions (e.g., a “T1 transition” where 2 sets of cells exchange neighbors). The morphogenetic capacity of current manmade materials is far from what biology can achieve. The long-term goal of this project is to build a tissue-like composite material, and apply biological morphogenesis principles to reconfigure the shape, structure, and function of the material. As a first step towards this goal, the specific aims of this research are to create a functional motif consisting of an inducible vesicle, and to demonstrate an elemental topological transition in these vesicles. The project is expected to advance knowledge at the interface of material science and synthetic and cell biology. It is expected to provide an experimental platform to investigate structured materials capable of relaying both chemical and mechanical signals, where microscopic, elemental topological transitions can be amplified to achieve macroscopic change in material morphology. This project represents the novel adaptation of biological principles in topological transitions towards material morphogenesis, and the identification of the minimal set of synthetic components and forces needed to drive a topological transition, by replacing a living cell with a minimal cell-free vesicle.

This project is supported to further expand the NSF 2026 Idea Machine winning entry "Engineered Living Materials".

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
Tissues are made up of many cells that interface and interact with each other to coordinate collective behavior. One type of collective behavior is tissue morphogenesis, where cells move together in a coordinated fashion to generate directed shape change in the tissue. In morphogenesis, cells drive topological transitions locally, such as by exchanging neighbors between two pairs of cells. When done in coordination in a network of many cells, the small-scale elemental topological transitions can create large-scale changes in the tissue shape and structure. While morphogenesis is common in biological tissues, most engineered materials are far from achieving the same degree of morphogenetic ability. Our long-term goal is to build a synthetic composite material that can harness the principles of morphogenesis to control the shape, structure, and function of the composite material.


As a first step, we engineered an elemental structure, similar in shape and size to a biological cell, that is capable of driving topological transitions in a network. To generate forces and initiate the motion required to drive a topological transition, we made each elemental structure from a stimuli-responsive hydrogel. We tested various methods for generating a large number of the elemental structures. Ultimately, we found that 3D printing using two-photon polymerization in a custom hydrogel material was the best way to control the shape of the structures and to generate cell-sized structures. Our second major outcome was the functionalization of the elemental structures with desired properties, such as the ability to form linkages. It was necessary to link pairs of elemental structures together to form a connected network. Our goal was to use DNA hybridization between complementary DNA strands conjugated to each element to form linkages. To that end, we demonstrated the use of maleimide-thiol conjugation chemistry to link thiolated DNA strands to the hydrogel that had been modified to incorporate terminal maleimide groups.


The result of our work is a platform for generating cell-like structures made of hydrogels that can be customized with desired geometries, material properties, and functionalities. Our work contributes to the broad goal of engineering living materials by harnessing interdisciplinary research expertise to advance the development of bioinspired materials science and engineering. This project allowed us to explore a variety of processes to generate cell-like structures and make progress toward our long-term vision of building novel materials that recapitulate the ability of biological cells to drive changes in the shape and structure of tissue. Additionally, this project provided opportunities for interdisciplinary research and training of multiple graduate students, including students who belong to groups typically underrepresented in STEM.

abstractText:
Sandy beaches represent a large fraction of the world’s unfrozen shoreline and they are under serious threat from sea level rise. They provide important ecosystem services including water filtration and nutrient cycling. These processes are controlled by a community of microorganisms working together called a microbiome in the beach subsurface. While we know the importance of microbiome activity in these systems, there are limited studies that characterize the microbial community in this environment. The goal of this project is to characterize the microbiome in the beach subsurface and investigate the environmental factors that control its structure and function. This goal will be achieved using next generation sequencing methods that provide vast amounts of genetic information from DNA and RNA sequences. Successful completion of this project will advance knowledge and understanding across different scientific fields including environmental microbiology, ecology, and environmental engineering and science. The proposed work will benefit society by furthering the understanding of the ecosystem services provided by beaches, information critical to understanding the impact of sea level rise on the environment. The diversity of the Nation’s STEM workforce will be increased by engaging college students from diverse backgrounds in the research. Further benefits to society will result from teaming with elementary school teachers to create learning modules on bacteria for school-aged children. The research team will also conduct outreach to the public during field work to educate them about the beach ecosystem and engage government officials on the issue of sea level rise.

The steep spatial physicochemical gradients and large temporal variation make the subterranean estuary of sandy beaches an ideal study system to focus on the goal of identifying the rules governing microbiome structure and function in coastal environments. This will be achieved by i) characterizing the microbiome in the subterranean estuary, ii) investigating the mechanisms controlling sandy beach microbiome dynamics, and iii) assessing microbial immigration via transport through the sands and local adaptation to changes in porewater chemistry. The research will employ state-of-the-science amplicon sequencing, metagenomics, and metatranscriptomics together with methods from hydrology and biogeochemistry. The research benefits society by furthering the understanding of the ecosystem services provided by beaches in terms of biogeochemical cycling. As beaches are threatened by sea level rise, this work is essential to fully anticipate the effects of sea level rise on the planet.

projectOutComesReport:
Sandy beaches represent between 31% of the planet's unfrozen shoreline. Sandy beaches provide essential ecosystem services including habitat for sensitive biota, protection of land from storm events and flooding, and water filtration and purification capacity. Beaches are also economically important because they provide a place for recreation and fishing. 

One of the most rapidly progressing research areas at sandy beaches involves the study of submarine groundwater discharge (SGD); groundwater discharge from coastal unconfined and confined aquifers to the sea. SGD from beaches provides an important flux of elements from land to sea. Forced by tides and waves, large volumes of seawater are flushed through the beach daily. In addition, meteoric groundwater can percolate through the beach discharging to the sea. In the subsurface of the beach is a subterranean estuary with steep chemical (salinity, oxygen, nutrient) and physical (temperature, moisture content) gradients. 

The beach can be viewed as a biogeochemical reactor. Studies have documented the changing oxidation state and form of nutrients, trace metals, and carbon within the subterranean estuary; and further, studies have shown how, coupled to the inflow and outflow of groundwater to the beach aquifer, these transformations affect the flux of elements to the coastal ocean. In some field studies, elemental fluxes from SGD are on par with those from large nearby river systems. However, has been little work to understand the role of microorganisms in mediating these processes.  

The research carried out in this project studied the microorganisms present in the lacunar environment between sand grains at the beach in the subterranean estuary. We documented a large diversity of microbes capable of nitrogen, sulfur and carbon cycling. These microbes are essential for mediating the biogeochemical reactions in the beach aquifer, and remove and change the form of nitrogen before groundwater discharges to the coastal ocean. We found that the rules of life governing the distribution of these organisms in the beach are biological, chemical, and physical. We found evidence that microorganism distribution can be controlled by waves and tides forcing movement of the microorganisms through the beach, and that changes in chemistry and other organisms present in the sands controls the distributions of organisms. 

Our work used the sandy beach as a model system for probing the rules of life. The steep chemical and physical gradients present at a beach control spatial and temporal variation in microbial communities over different scales. Additionally, the work led to greater insight into the roles of sandy beaches in global elemental cycling, which is urgently needed as their very existence is critically endangered by sea level rise. 

We collaborated and did outreach with the local communities, and we worked with graduate, undergraduate and middle school students from nearby communities.

abstractText:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this I-Corps project is the development of a software tool that would help teams to effectively manage changes and their negative impacts on project schedules and resources. The current inefficient management and lack of tools to minimize negative impacts from changes hurts the cash flow of a project and its stakeholders. Changes also delay projects significantly and lead to cost overruns. A recent study showed that the US construction industry spends $50 billion on change orders annually. Aside from the money spent on the direct cost of the change, such as materials and resources, much of these costs are wasted due to an inefficient use of time and lack of optimized planning procedures. Reducing the impacts of changes on duration and cost is paramount and may help construction companies to develop sustainability strategies for their projects and the environment.  Further, infrastructure projects funded by taxpayers’ money may leverage this tool as part of their value engineering mechanisms to gain more with the same level of resource allocation.

This I-Corps project is based on the development of an artificial intelligence (AI)-based visualization method that may assist project teams to effectively manage change events on any project. Current visualization tools do not have the capacity to analyze the impact of change orders on all three fronts:  temporal, spatial, and resources. The proposed method leverages the integrated approach towards schedule, workspace, and resources using advanced natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning to label and characterize change events data. These advanced AI-driven computational techniques may help project teams to visualize, review, and plan for changes within a fraction of time as compared to traditional methods. More specifically, this method visualizes the individual and cumulative direct and indirect impacts of change events on associated schedule activities using spaghetti graphs in which spaghetti lines and the change events are color coded by the usage of underlying resources. It also visualizes the utilization of space and resources, the underlying conflicts and over utilization due to the impacts of change events. The goal is to create an array of planning options to allow project teams to choose a sequence that minimizes both cost and duration impact.

projectOutComesReport:
Changes are inevitable but detrimental to the project performance if not appropriately planned and managed. Our preliminary studies show that changes alone can cause about 20% schedule overruns and a 12% increase in project cost. An average project team spends a cumulative of over 15 hours alone on managing a change over its lifetime.

ChangeVU is an end-to-end platform to manage changes on construction projects, from initiation to resolution. Our AI-based innovative technology will help reduce the turnover time from months to a couple of weeks, all with a click of a few buttons. Our vertically integrated system tracks the impact of changes in real-time. ChangeVU is compatible with phones, tablets, and laptops, enabling logging of change events from anywhere, on or off the field, and analyzing the result within a matter of seconds.

We are a couple of Stanford graduate students who developed the idea of ChangeVU to change the construction industry?s view on changes. We conducted extensive research on the industry pain points and wanted to validate our results by interviewing construction stakeholders. Our goal was to learn from the knowledge and experiences of these experts about the exact problems and frustrations around the state-of-practice change management processes.

We conducted over 100 interviews during the NSF workshop with experts ranging from VPs to field engineers. The highlights of these conversations are listed below:

  • -  Changes occur very frequently, and no systematic method is in place to assist the project teams in effectively incorporating changes into the ongoing work on the jobsites.

  • -  Smaller projects (<$25M) are manageable because the volume of changes is not much, and teams are small enough for better coordination. Mid-size projects (>$25M) and above are difficult to manage because of an increased volume of changes and coordination requirements within a larger team. Project teams spent 40-60% of their time dealing with them.

  • -  4/5 people experienced unexpected delays because of small changes.

  • -  75% of people indicated that no systematic resequencing of tasks is performed due to lack of

    time and a proper method to capture all changes.

  • -  80% of customers prefer web/app channels because they need to access them and get

    information on their phones. 100% of the customers want information on their phones and tablets, a platform that they can use from the site.

    Based on these results, we advanced our algorithms to assess the overall impact of all changes disregard of their size on three fronts: schedule, available space, and resources, may it be equipment, labor, or material. Using ChangeVU, the project teams will be able to plan changes in the most optimized manner and save more than 65% of time spent documenting, planning, and analyzing. ChangeVU seamlessly integrates with the project schedule, drawings, and 3D models to provide total control in real-time.

    With ChangeVU, our target customers (i.e., Project Managers) will benefit by a) creating change events on a single platform, b) analyzing its impact within a couple of minutes, c) visualizing the impact on the schedule, space, and resources, and discussing with your project team, d) creating an optimized execution plan to minimize cost and save time, and e) sharing the progress with clients and shareholders in real-time.

abstractText:
This award supports research in relativity and relativistic astrophysics and it addresses the priority areas of NSF's "Windows on the Universe" Big Idea. The detection of gravitational waves from coalescing black holes in 2015 launched the field of gravitational wave astronomy. Gravitational-wave detectors with a two-fold increase in sensitivity over Advanced LIGO would yield an order of magnitude increase in detection rate for black hole coalescences, and enable detection of fainter objects like binary neutron stars, greatly increasing their value for multi-messenger astronomy. All future detector upgrades and concepts rely on the development of new mirror coating materials to reduce thermal noise, which is the core research focus this collaborative project between Martin Fejer's group at Stanford University and Hai-Ping Cheng's group at the University of Florida. Reducing this noise source requires reducing the mechanical loss in the mirror coatings on the test masses. The goal of this project is to develop mirror coatings consistent with the mechanical and optical requirements for implementation in future generations of LIGO. Meeting this goal for room temperature detectors requires a solution of a longstanding problem in the physics of amorphous materials: understanding the nature of and finding means to reduce the low-energy excitations in amorphous metal oxides. On a longer time-scale, the proposed 3G detectors' cryogenic operation broadens the possible choice of low-noise mirror materials to include amorphous or crystalline semiconductors.

The mid-band sensitivity of the Advanced LIGO detectors is limited by thermal noise resulting from mechanical loss in the mirror coatings, and future upgrades including Advanced LIGO Plus will seek to reduce this source of noise by a factor of two or more. The Stanford-Florida partnership, alongside collaborators in the LSC Center for Coatings Research (CCR), has identified different structural motifs associated with room-temperature vs cryogenic mechanical losses, which led to synthesis of germania (GeO2) films, giving rise to the lowest-loss amorphous oxide film other than silica. Going forward, this structural guide, based on electron and x-ray scattering atomic structure data, will serve as a paradigm informing the development of high-refractive-index amorphous coatings with lower elastic loss. Atomic modeling of coating elastic loss combined with simulations of the coating deposition process will provide guidance for the selection of candidate materials, assist in interpretation of experimental structure data, and will ultimately assist in the design of synthesis experiments. Another long-standing effort at Stanford has been measurements of the absorption of low-optical-loss materials at the sub-ppm/cm level, dating back to the down select between silica and sapphire for initial LIGO test masses. The groups will continue to use the interferometric tool developed for those studies to characterize cryogenic losses in single-crystal silicon samples to evaluate their suitability for implementation in the Voyager technology demonstrator and future cryogenic detectors.

Addendum # 1

The Stanford-Florida Program in Support of LIGO on Coatings and Core Optics, a collaboration between Stanford University and the University of Florida, has focused its efforts on improving the technologies essential for the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) project, particularly in the development of low thermal noise mirror coatings and core optics. This initiative has brought together researchers and resources from both institutions to tackle the challenges of enhancing the sensitivity of gravitational wave detectors through advancements in optical technologies.

The project has achieved notable successes in the study and optimization of the atomic structures of amorphous mirror coatings. By developing atomic models for titanium-doped germanium dioxide (Ti:GeO2) coatings, the team has provided insights into how the microscopic structure of these coatings affects their mechanical loss properties, a critical factor in the performance of gravitational wave detectors.

One practical outcome of this research is the creation of a cryogenic mechanical loss measurement apparatus. This tool has allowed the measurement of how mechanical loss in various thin films changes with temperature, providing data that can help optimize the mirrors used in LIGO for better performance.

In addition to technological advancements, the program has offered valuable training and professional development opportunities for those involved. Students and researchers participating in the project have gained hands-on experience with cutting-edge technologies and methodologies, preparing them for future challenges in their careers.

The work conducted by the Stanford-Florida Program is grounded in scientific research and collaboration. Its contributions to the field of gravitational wave detection represent meaningful steps forward in the pursuit of understanding the universe. The findings and methodologies developed by the program have been shared with the wider scientific community, ensuring that the knowledge gained from this collaboration can benefit other researchers and projects in related fields.
